headline: Chinese President back in India after 7 years: What's on table for Modi-Xi talks
full_text:
Chinese President back in India after 7 years: What's on table for Modi-Xi talks
Xi Jinping's return to India after seven years will test whether the cautious thaw with Prime Minister Narendra Modi can evolve into a broader reset despite unresolved border, trade and strategic tensions.
Chinese President Xi Jinping will arrive in New Delhi on Saturday for the 18th BRICS Summit, making his first visit to India in seven years. The high-stakes engagement provides a major test of the cautious rapprochement between the two Asian powers after years of military confrontation and apparent diplomatic mistrust.
Xi’s visit, which comes amid efforts by India and China to normalise relations, will be closely watched for signs of whether the two countries can move beyond stabilisation of their ties towards a broader political and economic reset.
The Chinese president is expected to hold a bilateral meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at 6 pm on Saturday. The discussions are expected to cover the situation along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the wider boundary dispute and measures to expand trade and investment. The two sides seek to rebuild relations damaged by the 2020 military confrontation in eastern Ladakh.
The meeting assumes particular importance because Xi's last visit to India was in October 2019, when he held an informal summit with PM Modi in Mamallapuram near Chennai. Within months, the relationship deteriorated sharply following the deadly Galwan Valley clash in Ladakh in June 2020.
Since then, the two countries have spent years managing a military standoff, negotiating disengagement arrangements and maintaining diplomatic channels while economic relations also came under increasing strain.
The thaw that has emerged since 2024 has been cautious. Direct flights have resumed, some visa procedures have been eased, high-level political contacts have increased and the two sides have taken steps towards restoring border trade and people-to-people links.
But major obstacles remain. The unresolved boundary dispute, continued military deployments, strategic rivalry, a heavily unbalanced trade relationship and restrictions affecting investment, technology, equipment and business travel continue to constrain the relationship.
THE CRUCIAL SEVEN YEARS
Xi’s return to New Delhi comes after one of the most difficult phases in India-China relations in decades, marked by longstanding territorial disputes and deep strategic mistrust.
The frontier concerns remain unresolved, with the two militaries maintaining large deployments along their roughly 3,500-kilometre high-altitude border. The biggest setback came in 2020, when clashes in eastern Ladakh killed 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese soldiers.
The confrontation triggered a prolonged military standoff and a wider deterioration in political and economic ties. India tightened scrutiny of Chinese investments, restricted Chinese mobile applications and sought to reduce dependence on Chinese companies and technology.
For several years, both governments focused largely on military and diplomatic negotiations to prevent further escalation along the LAC.
A significant shift came in October 2024, when India and China reached an understanding on patrolling arrangements, clearing the way for renewed political engagement between PM Modi and Xi.
The two leaders subsequently held formal talks on the margins of the BRICS Summit in Kazan. PM Modi also visited China in August 2025, while direct flights resumed in October after more than five years. India eased visa procedures for Chinese business professionals, while both sides moved towards restoring border trade and allowing Indian pilgrims to resume the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra in Tibet.
Modi and Xi held further talks on the margins of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Tianjin in August 2025 and briefly interacted again at a regional forum in Kyrgyzstan earlier this month.
These steps have created a framework for a gradual thaw, but analysts remain cautious about calling it a full reset.
BORDER REMAINS AT THE HEART OF THE RELATIONSHIP
The Himalayan boundary remains the biggest challenge for Modi and Xi.
Both countries continue to maintain significant military forces along the frontier, making border management central to any normalisation effort. Recent diplomacy has focused on preventing incidents and creating mechanisms for longer-term negotiations.
In August, National Security Adviser Ajit Doval travelled to Beijing for the 25th round of Special Representatives' talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi. The discussions covered the boundary, maintaining peace and tranquillity along the border and broader measures to improve ties.
The two sides reached an eight-point consensus and agreed to advance discussions on an "Early and Substantial Harvest" involving boundary delimitation and border management. They have also discussed new Border Personnel Meeting Points and military hotlines.
Yet concerns persist over Chinese military activity in the eastern sector, including Arunachal Pradesh, which Beijing claims as "South Tibet" or "Zangnan". China has also renamed several locations in the region and issued maps claiming Arunachal Pradesh as its territory, moves that have drawn strong rejection from India.
On September 6, Indian and Chinese commanders held the first Corps Commander-level meeting in the eastern sector at the Vacha-Damai Border Personnel Meeting Point. The meeting followed reports of fresh Chinese military activity and alleged incursions in the Taksing area of Upper Subansiri district.
ECONOMIC TIES RESILIENT
The sharpest contradiction in India-China ties is economic. Despite political tensions, trade has remained resilient. China is India’s largest goods trading partner, with bilateral trade reaching USD 151 billion in the 2025-26 financial year.
But the relationship is heavily skewed towards China. India imported USD 131 billion worth of goods from China, while exports stood at only USD 19 billion, producing a record trade deficit of USD 112 billion.
New Delhi has responded by promoting domestic manufacturing and seeking to reduce dependence on Chinese machinery, electronics, chemicals and industrial components.
Yet Chinese technology, equipment and components remain important to several key sectors. India, according to experts, therefore faces a paradox. It wants to reduce strategic dependence on China while still relying on Chinese inputs to expand domestic production.
The challenge is not simply to increase trade, but to make the economic relationship more balanced and predictable.
WATER AND INFRASTRUCTURE CONCERNS
India's concerns with China also extend beyond the border. A major issue is Beijing's Medog hydropower project on the upper reaches of the Yarlung Tsangpo, which flows into India as the Brahmaputra.
China began construction in July 2025 on the project in Tibet near the Arunachal Pradesh border, with an estimated investment of 1 trillion yuan, or about USD 137 billion.
The project is slated for commercial operation in 2033, with planned capacity of 60,000 megawatts and annual generation of about 300 billion kilowatt-hours.
India have raised concerns and sought greater transparency and ecological information-sharing, while Beijing has not released a comprehensive environmental impact assessment.
The project adds to Indian concerns over Chinese infrastructure near the disputed frontier and developments on rivers flowing downstream into India and Bangladesh.
BRICS AND THE BIG PICTURE
Xi’s visit is taking place primarily in the context of the 18th BRICS Summit, giving his engagement with PM Modi a wider geopolitical dimension.
BRICS provides India and China with a common multilateral platform as both navigate an increasingly volatile international environment. According to Chinese officials, Xi's participation reflects Beijing's commitment to BRICS and to what it describes as a more inclusive global order.
The summit is expected to address intra-BRICS trade, payment systems, science and technology, climate change and coordination on major international issues.
Exprts note that for China, maintaining a working relationship with India strengthens the credibility and effectiveness of these wider global groupings, also including the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO). Beijing also sees BRICS as part of a broader effort to promote alternative institutions to those dominated by the United States.
India, however, has its own strategic calculations. New Delhi has deepened its security partnership with Washington and remains part of the Quad with the United States, Japan and Australia, an alignment Beijing views with suspicion.
India, meanwhile, remains concerned about China’s close relationship with Pakistan.
The result is a relationship where cooperation and competition coexist, where interests converge, while competing over security, technology, trade and regional influence, geopolitical experts observe.
THE US FACTOR
The changing international environment adds another layer to the PM Modi-Xi engagement.
Both India and China are dealing with volatile relations with the United States and the impact of American trade policies. This gives Beijing and New Delhi an incentive to maintain a functional relationship even where their strategic interests diverge.
Analysts argue that China's economic heft gives Beijing an opportunity to position itself as a reliable partner as both countries face the impact of US trade policies. Ashok Malik of The Asia Group has noted that Xi’s visit shows that, despite turbulence caused by the United States, India and China want to maintain a working relationship.
India’s partnership with Washington remains an important part of its security strategy, while China remains concerned about the Quad and India remains wary of Beijing’s ties with Pakistan.
TEST FOR PM MODI AND XI
The central question is no longer whether India and China want to talk. The real test is whether dialogue can generate enough confidence to address the obstacles that have accumulated since 2020.
A successful PM Modi-Xi meeting could provide momentum on border management, trade, investment and business mobility. The meeting between the leaders offers an opportunity to better align political and economic interests, although commercial ties will ultimately depend on the interests of businesses and citizens.
For India, the key test will be whether China can contribute to a more stable border while providing greater predictability in trade and technology flows. For China, the challenge will be convincing India that deeper economic engagement will not create additional strategic vulnerabilities.

headline: 28 foreigners lodged in Meghalaya jails despite completing sentence: Govt to court
full_text:
28 foreigners lodged in Meghalaya jails despite completing sentence: Govt to court
The officials assured the court that steps would be taken to repatriate the foreign nationals in coordination with the embassies concerned.
The Meghalaya government has told the high court that 28 foreign nationals are still lodged in jails across the state even after completing their sentences. It also said detention or holding centres would be identified within a week to house them until arrangements are made for their repatriation.
The submission was made before a division bench of Chief Justice Revati Mohite Dere and Justice W Diengdoh during the hearing of a case related to the detention of foreign nationals on Thursday. The state said it would file an affidavit setting out the steps to be taken after the detention or holding centres are identified.
Additional Advocate General K Khan made the submission before the bench. In compliance with the high court's September 9 order, Commissioner and Secretary, Home (Political) Department, Rosetta Mary Kurbah, Commissioner and Secretary, Home (Prisons), Ryntihlang Rapthap, Inspector General of Prisons Zenith Sangma, and SP-cum-Foreigners Registration Office Vivek Syiem appeared in person before the court.
The officials assured the court that steps would be taken to repatriate the foreign nationals in coordination with the embassies concerned. Khan also submitted a list of foreign nationals who have remained in jails beyond the completion of their sentences, and the court took it on record.
The court said the authorities, including the Meghalaya State Legal Services Authority, should assist the inmates in completing the formalities required for their return to their respective countries.
The bench also directed that help be provided for applying for the necessary documentation, including Foreigners Registration-related formalities, in cases where the foreign nationals have married Indian citizens and have children.
The matter has been listed for further hearing on September 17. In all, the case centres on the continued lodging of 28 foreign nationals in Meghalaya jails after their sentences ended and the steps being taken to move them to holding centres and complete the process for their repatriation.

headline: The High Court of Meghalaya has found 17 foreign nationals lodged in a Meghalaya jail despite having completed their sentences.
full_text:
The High Court of Meghalaya has found 17 foreign nationals lodged in a Meghalaya jail despite having completed their sentences.
Fifteen of these prisoners are Bangladeshi nationals, one is a Myanmar national, and one is a Nigerian.
A team assigned by the High Court visited the Shillong District Jail and found that the Myanmar national has been languishing behind bars for more than 10 years, while the Nigerian and the Bangladeshi nationals have spent between six months and a couple of years.
All the foreigners were lodged in the Shillong District Jail. The court team examined the condition of the prisoners and ascertained whether they were receiving the requisite facilities and legal aid.
Observing the plight of the foreign nationals while hearing a writ petition by the court’s Registrar General on Wednesday, (September 9, 2026), a Division Bench of Chief Justice Revati Mohite Dere and Justice Wanlura Diengdoh pulled up Additional Advocate General Khalid Khan for providing “completely misleading and incorrect” information about the condition of the prisons and prisoners through a letter on August 28.
During the hearing, amicus curiae T. Yangi B. said that during her prison visits, she found 11 prisoners who had completed their sentence in three other jails across Meghalaya. She, however, said she was not sure whether those prisoners were foreign nationals or Indians.
‘No detention centres’
The State’s Inspector General of Prisons informed the court that the prisoners have been kept in the jails past their sentence period as there are no detention centres in Meghalaya.
The court observed that the foreign nationals should have been moved to a temporary facility after the completion of their terms, as required by law. It directed the Additional Advocate General to take instructions on how soon a particular place could be designated as a detention centre until a proper one is established.
“We cannot countenance persons being incarcerated in jail, despite having completed their sentence. Of course, the question of compensation will be considered at an appropriate stage for all those who have been kept in prison beyond the period of sentence,” the court said.

headline: Supreme Court seeks Centre’s reply on curbs on social media use by minors
full_text:
Supreme Court seeks Centre’s reply on curbs on social media use by minors
Issuing notice on a petition filed by a non-profit child rights body, a bench headed by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant said, “There is need for some safeguards in India. Some firewall is necessary for protecting our children.”
The Supreme Court on Thursday sought the Centre’s response on a petition seeking restrictions on social media use by minors, observing that “firewalls” are necessary to safeguard the rights of children.
Issuing notice on a petition filed by a non-profit child rights body, a bench headed by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant said, “There is need for some safeguards in India. Some firewall is necessary for protecting our children.”
The court made the observation while hearing a petition filed by Just Rights for Children Alliance which pointed out that social media intermediaries and digital platforms allow persons above 13 years to open accounts. It argued that minors are incapable of entering into any contract as the Indian Contract Act summarily declares a minor’s consent for an agreement to be void right from the time such an agreement comes into existence.
The bench, also comprising justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, agreed that the matter requires to be examined as the petition highlighted various instances of how minors are being subjected to crimes, sexual exploitation, cyberbullying, and trafficking on various digital platforms.
The petition, argued by senior advocate HS Phoolka said, “It is well settled that an agreement entered into by a person who was a minor on the date of execution is void ab initio under section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Yet, we are seeing that children below 18 years are permitted to independently create and maintain accounts on social-media platforms and access digital platforms.”
It stated that opening of an account on social media or digital platforms requires children to accept terms of service, user agreement, privacy policies, etc and this cannot be permitted when the law in the country does not recognise the right of a person below 18 years to enter any contract.
However, the plea made an exception for permitting access to lawful, educational and age-appropriate digital content through accounts maintained and controlled by their parents or lawful guardians, subject to an appropriate regulatory framework.
Phoolka stated that the issue also raises privacy concerns. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act 2023 recognises the special vulnerability of children and requires verifiable parental or guardian consent for processing personal data of a child. Even the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 are silent on the contractual capacity of a minor to access and use the services of social media intermediaries or digital platforms.
The petition urged the Centre to step in and declare all such accounts opened by children to be void. Till such time the guidelines are framed in this regard by the Centre under the 2021 IT Rules, the petition requested the court to pass a direction restricting any digital platform from entering into a contract with a child under 18 years.
The issue of restricting social media usage by children has been viewed with seriousness across jurisdictions. Australia has passed a law completely banning minors below 16 years from holding social media accounts. There is no parental consent exception provided under the law and the liability of social media intermediaries is made absolute with any violation inviting heavy penalty on them to the tune of $50 million. However, the law makes exceptions for learning platforms such as WhatsApp Messenger Kids, YouTube Kids and Google Classroom.
A similar law has also been passed by Malaysia and Indonesia which bans social media use by minors below the age of 16 with no parental consent exception provided. Malaysian law applies to platforms having at least 8 million Malaysian users. With regard to Indonesia, there is no such clause but it applies to “high-risk” platforms where minors may be exposed to harmful and sensitive content.
In the United Arab Emirates, the restriction applies to minors below 15 years of age and for those in the age bracket of 15 to 16, age-appropriate content controls are recommended. Even in the United States, for users below 13 years, verifiable parent consent is required.
Besides, several countries including the United Kingdom, Canada have proposed ban on social media use by persons below 16 years but the same has not yet been implemented.

NEW DELHI: For the first time in 8 years, an Iranian president will visit India with Masoud Pezeshkian set to arrive in New Delhi for the 18th BRICS summit on Friday, amid escalating West Asia tensions that have cast a shadow over the summit. Shortly after his arrival, Pezeshkian will participate in the BRICS Business Forum meeting along with PM Narendra Modi, Russian President Vladimir Putin and other leaders before joining Modi for a bilateral in the evening.The last Iranian president to visit India was Hassan Rouhani in 2018. While Iran has confirmed participation by the president in the BRICS summit, Saudi Arabia and the UAE - both parties to the West Asia conflict along with Tehran - will be represented by foreign minister Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud and Abu Dhabi crown prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan respectively.Pezeshkian is likely to reiterate his message before Modi for India to help end the war and suitably address Tehran's concerns related to the current situation, including through a strong condemnation of "illegal aggression" against Iran, in the proposed BRICS declaration. In his meetings with both Putin and Pezeshkian on Friday, Modi is expected to stress the need for new members to subscribe to consensus in the grouping on critical issues and work together for a unified joint declaration.
India agreed to the recent SCO Bishkek Declaration that condemned attacks on Iran. The declaration did not name the US or Israel though to prevent any resistance from members that have also cultivated ties with Washington.However, with the presence of UAE in BRICS, balancing the interests of both sides has not been easy for Indiaâs BRICS chairship. Itâs unlikely that the UAE will agree to an SCO-like formulation without seeking an explicit condemnation of Iranian attacks.
Gulf states like the UAE and Saudi Arabia are only dialogue partners in SCO.India will prioritise the UN Charter, dialogue and diplomacy, freedom of navigation and civilian protection in the declaration. If the deadlock persists, the government will look to insulate economic agreements from the West Asia discord by acknowledging respective national positions.The BRICS foreign ministersâ meeting earlier this year ended without a consensual statement, with Tehran adamant on a condemnation of the alleged violation of international law by the US and Israel and accusing the UAE of being directly involved in aggression against Iran.

headline: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Friday (September 11, 2026) slammed the Congress and other Opposition parties for creating a "negative atmosphere" around the BRICS summit, alleging that they are unable to "digest" India's progress as the country ...

The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Friday (September 11, 2026) slammed the Congress and other Opposition parties for creating a "negative atmosphere" around the BRICS summit, alleging that they are unable to "digest" India's progress as the country moves forward.
The ruling party said that while in 2011-12, under the Congress-led UPA government, India appeared to be losing its position within BRICS, today all BRICS' heads of state are in India, and the country is celebrating the bloc "as never before." India is hosting the 18th BRICS Summit on September 12-13 at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi. A day earlier, the Congress questioned the benefits of hosting the BRICS Summit.
In a video message, BJP MP and national spokesperson Sambit Patra said that while the "I" in BRIC was "turning shaky" in 2011-12, India is now one of the strongest partners of BRICS. "Today, India has found its position in the global arena as never before," he said.
"Remember, the 'I' in BRICS stands for India, and the 'I' in India stands for the 140 crore people of India. I am India. I am one of the strongest partners of BRICS, and I am proud of it. Today, I am proud to be a citizen of India and a very strong member of BRICS," he added. Mr. Patra cited two articles published in leading newspapers in 2011 and 2012 to back his claim.
"Today, the Congress party and some Opposition parties are trying to spread negativity and create a negative atmosphere around the BRICS Summit. I think they need to be shown a mirror," he said.
Citing a 2012 article based on comments by global financial services firm Goldman Sachs, Mr. Patra said its headline was "India least attractive BRICS member in valuation terms." "Goldman Sachs clearly says that in 2012, if there was one BRIC member that was the least attractive in terms of valuation, it was India," Mr. Patra said.
He said when Jim O'Neill, then chairman of Goldman Sachs, was asked whether Brazil was the strongest BRIC country and India the weakest, he said India was the least attractive in terms of valuation.
"China would be the most attractive; India would be relatively the least... That being said, because the markets are so worried about India, as I mentioned earlier, if we do indeed get some reforms, perhaps India will further rally ahead of the move than the other markets. I have China as number one, probably right now, Brazil as number two, Russia is number three, and India is number four," Mr. Patra quoted O'Neill as saying.
He further said the final line of the article stated that it would not be a surprise if Indonesia replaced India, as Indonesia had moved far ahead.
"What is the essence of this article? It essentially says that in 2012, there were no meaningful reforms in India, the country was falling behind, inflation was high, and the condition of the Indian market was such that, among the BRIC nations, India was at the bottom," he said.
Mr. Patra said the second article, published on September 21, 2011, highlighted high inflation and a weak currency in India. "The second article is dated September 21, 2011, and its headline is, 'With high inflation and weak currency, India not like other BRIC countries'," he said.
"Inflation in India is the worst among the so-called BRIC nations. Current account deficit is a concern, fiscal deficit is a worry, fresh investments are stalled despite creaky infrastructure. Probably for the first time in a decade since Jim O'Neill of Goldman Sachs coined the acronym, BRIC is weakening and the ‘I’ in it turning shaky," Mr. Patra said, quoting further from the second article.
"And yet, we have some politicians and some Opposition leaders who are not able to digest this. Today, some members of the Opposition and the Congress party are unable to digest India's progress because India is moving forward," Mr. Patra added.

headline: Mumbai-based Air India pilot dies in Delhi hotel hours before flying
full_text:
Mumbai-based Air India pilot dies in Delhi hotel hours before flying
The pilot had earlier worked with Air India Express and moved to Air India a couple of months ago.
An Air India pilot died in Delhi after he was found unconscious at a hotel where he was staying during a layover, the airline said on Saturday, adding that it is extending all support to the deceased's family.
The Mumbai-based pilot was on a layover at a hotel in Vasant Kunj area of Delhi when he was found unconscious last evening. He was immediately rushed to a hospital, where he was declared dead.
According to sources, the pilot was scheduled to operate a Delhi-Seoul flight, which would have been his second flight for Air India.
Sources added that a heart attack is suspected to be the cause of death.
Also Read: Air India’s one too many ‘impossible’ incidents
The pilot had earlier worked with Air India Express and moved to Air India a couple of months ago. He was scheduled to operate a flight early this morning.
The pilot had been associated with the Air India Express group since 2004-05. His brother was also with the group, and the two were from the same batch. Their father had worked as a member of the cabin crew. The pilot's brother was undergoing conversion training to fly the Boeing 787.
Air India ‘deeply saddened’ by pilot's death
Air India said it was “deeply saddened” by his passing and is in close touch with his family, extending all support to them at this time of grief.
Delhi Police said a PCR call was received at PS Vasant Kunj North on Friday regarding the ill health of a guest at a hotel in Vasant Kunj. Police reached the spot and found the person unconscious and unresponsive, according to a statement shared by news agency ANI.
The man was shifted to a hospital, where he was declared brought dead, Delhi Police was quoted as saying.
The Crime Team was subsequently called to the spot. The deceased was working as a captain with an airline and had checked into the hotel on September 10, police said.
“On the evening of September 11, his brother contacted the hotel manager and informed him that his brother was not responding to his calls. The manager went to the room, which was locked from the inside, and opened it with the hotel master key, where the deceased was found unconscious and unresponsive. The post-mortem examination was conducted at Safdarjung Hospital on September 12,” Delhi Police said.
Police said the cause of death will be ascertained after the final opinion is received. Further inquiry is underway, and inquest proceedings under Section 194 of the BNSS are being conducted, they said.

headline: India forged a consensus of BRICS countries on Saturday (September 12, 2026), after Iran and the United Arab Emirates agreed to a last-minute compromise on the language used about the war in West Asia, allowing the 11-member grouping to adopt the New...
full_text:
India forged a consensus of BRICS countries on Saturday (September 12, 2026), after Iran and the United Arab Emirates agreed to a last-minute compromise on the language used about the war in West Asia, allowing the 11-member grouping to adopt the New Delhi Declaration at a meeting chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The statement — that did not directly mention the attacks against Iran by the United States and Israel nor Iran’s subsequent strikes on its Persian Gulf neighbours, including the UAE — called for “maximum restraint” in the war. It made no separate mention of the Russian war in Ukraine.
The meeting was attended by the leaders of eight member countries, including Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, and the leaders of Indonesia, Ethiopia, Egypt, and South Africa. Brazil and the UAE sent high-level representatives.
‘Not against anyone’
Addressing the leaders, Mr. Modi said that 20 years after the grouping of emerging economies was originally formed, BRICS was “coming of age” with a “distinct identity” not aimed against others on the global stage.
“We respect each other’s perspectives and move forward through consensus. We strive to move ahead with an approach that is not against anyone but instead seeks to take everyone along,” the Prime Minister said, in a possible reference to the criticism of BRICS in the U.S. as an “anti-western” grouping.
Mr. Modi suggested that BRICS build a “troika” system like the G-20, so incoming and outgoing Presidents of the grouping bring continuity to discussions. He also proposed a roadmap for global governance reform, a seafarer distress network, and a BRICS global south mechanism for skill development in new technologies. The New Delhi declaration called for “comprehensive reform” of the United Nations, including support for Brazil and India to get a bigger role in the Security Council.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, who held an hour-long bilateral meeting with Mr. Modi after the session, announced that China would take over the presidency of BRICS for the next year. The grouping had become the “world’s most influential platform for cooperation among emerging markets and developing countries,” he said.
Delicate diplomacy
The joint declaration also called for the protection of civilians and expressed “deep concern” over attacks on civilian infrastructure and nuclear facilities in West Asia, in a reference to the U.S. and Israel’s missile strikes in Iran.
The paragraphs on the war in Iran took delicate diplomacy by Indian negotiators at “various levels”, said officials, and was forged after overnight negotiations and talks between Mr. Modi and the leaders of Iran, Russia, and the UAE. In a rare diplomatic breakthrough, Iran’s President, Mr. Pezeshkian met with the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi Khaled bin Mohamed Al Nahyan on the sidelines of the summit at Delhi’s Bharat Mandapam official venue.
Strong criticism of Israel
Significantly, given India’s close ties with Israel and Mr. Modi’s own visit to Jerusalem in February, the grouping declared its strong criticism of Israel for its bombardment of Gaza. It expressed support for South Africa’s case against Israel in international courts, calling for the provision of humanitarian aid in Gaza, where more than 70,000 civilians are believed to have been killed.
In addition, it supported a two-state solution for Palestine, with full rights at the UN, 1967 borders, and East Jerusalem as its capital. In an extended 8-paragraph reference to Israeli actions, it slammed the “forced displacement, temporary or permanent, under any pretext, of any of the Palestinian population from the Occupied Palestinian Territory”.
It also criticised the U.S. blockade of Cuba, and expressed concern over violence in Sudan.
On economic issues, the BRICS countries resolved to increase intra-BRICS trade and payments in national currencies. Taking aim at the U.S. for its tariffs and western countries for their unilateral sanctions, the joint statement said that BRICS countries “condemned the imposition of unilateral coercive measures that are contrary to international law”.
Compromise and consensus
Previous ministerial meetings of BRICS this year had failed to issue joint statements on the Iran-UAE tussle. Sources privy to the negotiations said that Iran had wanted a strong condemnation of the U.S. and Israel for starting the war with strikes that assassinated its Supreme Leader, similar to the statement issued by the SCO grouping, which does not include the UAE. The UAE wanted “equal condemnation” of Iran’s attacks against its neighbours. Eventually, the text agreed to included non-specific references to the conflict.
The consensus was achieved through months of “threadbare” discussions, according to Sudhakar Dalela, Indian Sherpa at the talks and Secretary (Economic Relations) in the Ministry of External Affairs. He was addressing a media briefing after the closed BRICS session on the future of global governance and strengthening multilateralism. Side-stepping a question from The Hindu on whether India had asked for support from other leaders in BRICS to help convince Iran and UAE to agree to the draft language, he said that the cooperation and collaboration of all members was “key”.
“In preparation of the BRICS summit, we have been discussing the Middle East situation (West Asia) for some time. In a grouping where members have diverse experiences, it is important to allow members to have a shared forum, and within that framework to build consensus,” Mr. Dalela said. He also underlined BRICS countries’ consensus against cross-border terrorism, with a specif reference to the Pahalgam terror attack in 2025.
On Sunday, Mr. Modi will chair a session of BRICS Plus countries and regional representatives for an outreach session that will include the leaders of Malaysia, Uzbekistan, Uganda, Vietnam, and Kazakhstan.

headline: How India pulled off BRICS consensus on Delhi declaration amid West Asia crisis

How India pulled off BRICS consensus on Delhi declaration amid West Asia crisis
The Brics leaders endorsed New Delhi’s long-standing position that “dialogue and diplomacy” are the only options to settle conflicts
India pulled off a diplomatic victory at the Brics Summit on Saturday with the adoption of a consensus joint declaration despite divergences between Iran and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) over the West Asia crisis, though the document was shorn of any references to the war and only spoke of dialogue and diplomacy to resolve conflicts.
Members of the diverse grouping agreed to the final text of the Brics New Delhi Declaration, especially the paragraph referring to the situation in West Asia, late Saturday afternoon, hours before the document was unveiled around 4:30 pm, people familiar with the matter said.
Also Read | ‘Differences should not become disputes’: PM Modi tells Xi peace on border key to India-China ties
Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the adoption of the declaration at the end of the opening day’s deliberations in the presence of Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
Deep Dive
Also Read: PM Modi, Xi welcome ‘steady progress’ in India-China ties at BRICS meet
The Brics leaders endorsed New Delhi’s long-standing position that “dialogue and diplomacy” are the only options to settle conflicts and stressed the need for joint efforts to ensure the flow of global trade and energy. The declaration was adopted on the opening day of the two-day summit, capping uncertainty created by the sharp divisions between Iran and the UAE that held up joint statements at several preparatory meetings in recent months. Brics operates on consensus, and objections from any member state could have blocked a joint declaration.
The crucial paragraph on West Asia expressed “deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions” in the region and called for maximum restraint and “avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation”. There was no direct reference to Iran in the context of the conflict, or the US and Israeli attacks on Iran in February that triggered the conflict.
The declaration called for ensuring the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure in line with the UN Charter, including respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states.
“We encourage increasing efforts, through dialogue and diplomacy, towards a long-term understanding that will contribute to lasting peace, security and stability in the region,” the declaration said. “We stress the need to work together to maintain smooth flow of global trade, supply chains and energy, in accordance with applicable international law.”
Several factors contributed to India’s efforts to forge consensus on the joint declaration, including getting Iran and the UAE to shift from their earlier demands seeking condemnation of attacks on their territories, the Russian side seeking the toning down of language on conflicts that could be perceived as a reference to the situation in Ukraine, and renewed efforts by Iran to mend fences with key players in West Asia, the people said.
Pezeshkian met Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on the margins of the Brics Summit on Saturday, and Iran plans to meet members of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and Iraq in Oman on September 14 to discuss an agreement on transit through the Strait of Hormuz. This will be the first such meeting since the start of the West Asia conflict.
Ajay Srivastava of the economic think tank Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) said the declaration, without naming the US, Israel or Iran, had sent a “clear and carefully balanced message that the US and Israel should avoid attacking Iran, Iran should refrain from retaliatory strikes against neighbouring Gulf states such as the UAE, and all parties must protect civilians, respect sovereignty and pursue dialogue and diplomacy”.
The call to maintain the smooth flow of global trade and energy is significant as it is a call to the US and its allies to avoid military action that could obstruct the critical global energy corridor of the Strait of Hormuz, Srivastava said. “Given Brics’ conflicting interests and internal constraints, securing consensus on such a clear position represents a diplomatic win for India,” he said.
Also Read | BRICS nations condemn Pahalgam attack, seek action against terror safe havens
Diplomatic observers, however, noted that the New Delhi Declaration was different from the declarations at the Brics Summits in Russia in 2024 and in Brazil in 2025 in that it made no direct references to the conflicts in Iran and Ukraine. The Rio de Janeiro Declaration, for instance, condemned the military strikes against Iran in June 2025, and also recalled national positions on the conflict in Ukraine.
The declaration expressed deep concern at the continued violence in Gaza despite a ceasefire and urged all parties to maintain the truce and ensure unhindered humanitarian access in the region. “We call for halting any policies aimed at forced displacement of Palestinians from Gaza Strip and express concern regarding arrangements that may prejudice the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people and legitimise or prolong occupation,” the declaration said.
It said a just and lasting solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict can be achieved only through peaceful means and the fulfilment of the legitimate rights of Palestinians. Expressing unwavering commitment to a two-state solution, the declaration called for the establishment of a sovereign, independent and viable state of Palestine with East Jerusalem as its capital.
Also Read | PM Modi, Putin and Xi hold hands at BRICS summit in a powerful show of unity
Brics also endorsed India’s zero-tolerance policy towards all forms of terrorism and the shunning of double standards in countering terror, with the declaration backing a concerted approach in dealing with the challenge. The declaration condemned in the “strongest terms” the Pahalgam terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir in 2025 that killed 26 people.
The grouping also criticised the proliferation of “trade-restrictive actions that are inconsistent with WTO rules, whether in the form of indiscriminate rising of tariffs and non-tariff measures, or protectionism under the guise of environmental objectives.”
“We voice serious concerns about the rise of unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures which distort trade and are inconsistent with WTO rules,” it said.
In the context of economic cooperation, which has emerged as one of the key pillars of Brics, the declaration noted that the multilateral trading system was at a crossroads and the proliferation of trade-restrictive actions inconsistent with WTO rules, including “indiscriminate rising of tariffs and non-tariff measures, or protectionism under the guise of environmental objectives”, threatens to further reduce global trade, disrupt supply chains and introduce uncertainty into international trade activities.
“We voice serious concerns about the rise of unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures which distort trade and are inconsistent with WTO rules,” the declaration said, adding that Brics states will work to enhance WTO’s responsiveness to trade disruptions and the priorities of emerging markets and developing economies.
Without naming the US, the declaration condemned unilateral coercive measures, including economic sanctions and secondary sanctions, and said such actions negatively impact the rights to development, health, and food security of targeted states, disproportionately affect people in vulnerable situations, and deepen the digital divide.

Priyank Kharge backs Karnataka's 2 stanzas 'Vande Mataram' directive: 'Do we need patriotism lessons from...'
He cites guidance from historical leaders and criticizes the BJP's motives, questioning their patriotism amidst ongoing economic concerns.
State home minister Priyank Kharge on Friday defended the state’s decision to restrict Vande Mataram to two stanzas at most state government functions.
He said the state government had no reason to revise its decision merely because the BJP had objected to it. He said the Congress was following an approach established by senior national leaders and rejected the suggestion that the party needed to prove its patriotism. “We had gone by what eight to 10 senior leaders like Rabindranath Tagore, Subhas Chandra Bose, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Gandhiji, Nehru decided and told us to follow. Are these people (BJP) bigger than them?” he said.
Also Read | ‘Should Kashmiris be jailed?’ Omar Abdullah's sharp reply to Congress amid Vande Mataram row
The order provides for the first two stanzas to be sung at state government events. It does not apply to events attended by the President, Vice President, Prime Minister or Governor.
The decision has come against the backdrop of a directive by the Union Home Ministry in January, when the Centre said all six stanzas of Vande Mataram should be sung before the national anthem when the two were played together. The directive formed part of events marking 150 years of Vande Mataram.
The Congress Working Committee decided in August to adhere to a 1937 resolution under which two stanzas of the song would be sung at party programmes. “Do we need to take lessons on patriotism from those who took a ₹60 pension from the British?” said Kharge.
Also Read | Vande Mataram: The first proclamation of cultural nationalism
The BJP has described the Karnataka order as minority appeasement. Union minister Pralhad Joshi said Vande Mataram had a central place in the freedom struggle and deserved due respect. Joshi also warned that the party could face political consequences in the 2028 Assembly elections. Kharge, however, questioned why the Centre had chosen to prescribe all six stanzas now, despite the party having governed at the Centre for years. “Unable to speak about the economic situation, employment, NEET exam irregularities, or what is happening at the public service commissions, they are bringing up such things to cover up all these issues,” he said.

headline: Putin's 'Doomsday Plane' in Delhi: Why this luxurious, Soviet era aircraft is named so?
full_text:
Putin's 'Doomsday Plane' in Delhi: Why this luxurious, Soviet era aircraft is named so?
Putin’s “Flying Kremlin” has arrived in India for the BRICS Summit. Here’s what makes the presidential aircraft so unique and secure.
Russian president Vladimir Putin arrived in Delhi on September 11, for the 18th BRICS Summit aboard one of the most heavily guarded aircraft in the world— the specially modified Ilyushin Il-96-300PU, popularly known as the “Flying Kremlin” or, in some reports, Putin’s “Doomsday Plane”.
Putin is in India for a three-day visit during which, he is holding talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and attending the BRICS summit.
Why is it called a ‘Doomsday Plane’?
Vladimir Putin’s “Flying Kremlin”, also referred to as the "Doomsday Plane” is a modified version of the Ilyushin Il-96-300, a long-range, four-engine Russian airliner developed by the Ilyushin Design Bureau in the 1980s. With its roots in the Soviet era, the aircraft remains one of the most distinctive presidential jets in the world.
Deep Dive
The Il-96-300PU is not Russia’s dedicated “Doomsday Plane”. According to a report by OneIndia, that designation is generally associated with the Ilyushin Il-80, which was specifically developed as an airborne command post designed to maintain strategic command and control during a nuclear conflict or other major national emergency. The Il-96-300PU used by Putin is primarily a presidential command and transport aircraft.
Its importance lies in allowing the Russian president to continue communicating securely while airborne, even during situations in which conventional communications could be compromised.
Also Read | Xi Jinping's car arrives in Delhi under black covers. What we know about the 'secret' Hongqi N701
Two identical planes for Putin’s security
One of the most striking aspects of Putin’s aircraft arrangements is the use of two identical Il-96-300PU aircraft. According to a report by NDTV, both aircrafts were used during his journey to India, with the planes flying simultaneously.
The tactic is intended to make it difficult for outsiders to determine which aircraft is carrying Putin. Both jets have a similar appearance, making the president’s exact location harder to identify.
What makes the aircraft different?
The Il-96-300PU combines the characteristics of a long-range presidential aircraft with those of a secure command centre. Its communications equipment is considered among its most important features, allowing the Russian leadership to maintain contact while travelling.
Reports have also highlighted electronic countermeasures and other defensive systems aboard the aircraft, including radar-jamming technology and infrared countermeasures. However, details of its exact capabilities remain classified, and some claims about the aircraft’s defensive capabilities have not been independently verified.
Also Read | Putin takes a dig at 'so-called' G7, stresses BRICS nations' 40% share of world GDP
What amenities are available in the aircraft?
The Il-96-300PU is equipped with a private presidential suite featuring a bedroom, a spacious conference room with boardroom-style seating, a private office and a guest lounge. It also has dedicated dining and kitchen areas, along with a medical compartment. Some media reports have also claimed that the aircraft includes a fitness area to accommodate the president’s exercise routine.
The cabin is finished with gold-plated accents, rich woodwork featuring rare Karelian birch, neoclassical furnishings, premium leather upholstery and ornate tapestries, giving the aircraft an opulent, mansion-like ambience rather than the feel of a conventional jet.
Putin’s aircraft in Delhi
Putin’s arrival has drawn attention during the BRICS Summit, where leaders of major emerging economies are meeting in New Delhi. His aircraft landed at Palam Air Force Station amid extensive security arrangements surrounding the Russian president’s visit.
Also Read | Russia ready to contribute to global energy, food security, Putin pledges at BRICS
The aircraft’s presence in India has therefore become a talking point in its own right — not simply because of its luxury or appearance, but because it represents the extraordinary level of security and communications infrastructure surrounding one of the world’s most closely protected leaders.

headline: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday met Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi, where the two leaders welcomed the “steady progress” in India-China relations since their last meeting in August 2025.
full_text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday met Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi, where the two leaders welcomed the “steady progress” in India-China relations since their last meeting in August 2025.
“We reviewed the full range of India-China relations. Also conveyed best wishes for China’s BRICS presidency that commences next year,” said Mr. Modi in a message after the meeting.
“The two leaders welcomed the steady progress in India-China bilateral relations since their last meeting in Tianjin in August 2025. They reaffirmed that both countries should take a strategic and long-term perspective of their ties. Differences should not become disputes,” the External Affairs Ministry said in a statement after the talks.
Mr. Modi stressed the importance of “peace and tranquillity” in the border areas, describing the matter as “essential basis for development of bilateral relations”.
The MEA said the two leaders expressed their commitment to “a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question”, proceeding from the political perspective of their overall bilateral relations and the long-term interests of the two peoples.
A Chinese Foreign Affairs Ministry statement said, “They [India and China] should pursue progress on bilateral relations and the boundary question in parallel, ensuring that each supports the other, and maintain peace and tranquillity in border areas.”
The meeting came a fortnight after the conclusion of the 2026 Kailash Manasarovar Yatra, which began following an improvement in bilateral ties over the past two years that increased people-to-people relations and cross-border trade through Himalayan passes.
Mr. Xi last met Mr. Modi in August 2025 on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Tianjin, building on a similar meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in October 2024 in Kazan, Russia. These dialogues have indicated a gradual improvement in ties that had entered a cold phase following the 2020 Galwan clashes in eastern Ladakh.
Mr. Xi arrived with a large delegation earlier in the day for a two-day visit and was driven to the summit venue at Bharat Mandapam amid tight security.
Strategic perspective
Chinese State media reported that Mr. Xi said the two states have “different national circumstances”, but “China and India can learn from each other’s strengths and achieve shared development”. Mr. Xi outlined four points on how to ensure the long-term, steady development of India-China relations and emphasised “rational strategic understanding”, “cooperation through mutual benefit”, “mutual respect and understanding”, and “openness and inclusiveness through multilateral cooperation” in the UN, SCO, BRICS, and G20.
The MEA said the two leaders agreed that both sides “must continue to expand common ground” in resolving “regional and global issues” while “addressing challenges”.
West Asia
Speaking at the summit on the situation in West Asia, Mr. Xi said the war has inflicted “serious losses” on the people of all countries in the region, and it is against the common interests of the international community. Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning, referring to Mr. Xi’s speech, called for a “political settlement” of the crisis. “China will work with fellow BRICS members to play a due role in bringing peace and tranquillity to the Middle East,” said Mr. Xi, referring to India and China as “key members of the Global South” with “significant responsibilities” in world affairs.
“We must keep the future of humanity and the well-being of our people at heart, join hands to drive high-quality cooperation within the expanded BRICS framework, advocate for an equal and orderly multipolar world and an economic globalisation that is universally beneficial and inclusive, and inject greater positive energy into promoting global peace, stability, development, and prosperity,” he said.
Mr. Xi said BRICS has demonstrated “vigorous vitality” over the past two decades and has become the “most influential cooperation platform for emerging markets and developing countries in the world today”. He said BRICS countries have overcome numerous challenges working together, including the “international financial crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic and climate change”.

headline: PM Modi holds bilateral meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping on sidelines of BRICS summit

PM Modi holds bilateral meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping on sidelines of BRICS summit
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a bilateral meeting lasting more than 50 minutes in New Delhi on Saturday, shortly after the adoption of the Brics Summit 2026 declaration.The meeting took place on the sidelines of the Brics Summit, where leaders of the grouping adopted the summit declaration following discussions on key global and regional issues.
Welcoming Xi, PM Modi thanked China for its support and cooperation during India's Brics chairmanship and said the two sides now had an opportunity to discuss bilateral ties."It gives me great pleasure to extend a warm welcome to you. Thank you very much for your positive remarks at the Brics Summit. I express my gratitude for the support and cooperation received from China during India's Brics chairmanship. We now have the opportunity to discuss bilateral cooperation. Once again, a warm welcome to India."The meeting assumes significance as India and China have sought to stabilise bilateral relations following tensions along their disputed border in recent years. The two leaders have held several engagements aimed at improving ties and maintaining peace and tranquillity along the border.
PM Modi welcomes Xi
During the bilateral meeting, PM Modi expressed his gratitude for China's cooperation during India's Brics presidency and welcomed Xi to India.Also read: PM Modi, Xi & Putin meet for 3rd time in 3 yrs; PM shares photo"I express my gratitude for the support and cooperation received from China during India's Brics chairmanship. We now have the opportunity to discuss bilateral cooperation. Xi stresses long-term ties

Both sides should keep the future of humanity in mind and the well-being of their peoples at heart, and work together to advance high-quality cooperation within the greater BRICS framework. We should advocate an equal and orderly multipolar world and an inclusive, mutually beneficial form of economic globalisation, injecting more positive energy into the promotion of world peace, stability, development and prosperity."
Earlier, the BRICS nations unanimously adopted the New Delhi Declaration 2026, which expressed deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in West Asia and called for maximum restraint and avoidance of actions that could further aggravate the situation.âWe urge to ensure the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure in accordance with the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations in their entirety and interconnectedness, including respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the States,â the declaration said.The BRICS declaration also encouraged greater efforts through dialogue and diplomacy towards a long-term understanding contributing to lasting peace, security and stability in the region.âWe stress the need to work together to maintain smooth flow of global trade, supply chains and energy, in accordance with applicable international law,â it said.The grouping expressed serious concern over deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities under full safeguards of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), stressing that nuclear safeguards, safety and security must be upheld, including during armed conflicts.The declaration also called for implementation of relevant UN General Assembly and UN Security Council resolutions and urged all parties to ensure the maintenance of ceasefire and full and unhindered humanitarian access in the Gaza Strip.Addressing the BRICS Summit, Xi Jinping called on BRICS nations to play a peacemaking role amid the conflict in West Asia, saying China would work with other members towards that goal.The BRICS declaration also noted the current global context of polarisation and distrust and encouraged global action to strengthen international peace and security. It advocated a multilateral approach that respects diverse national viewpoints on key global issues, including sustainable development, eradication of hunger and poverty and the global response to climate change.
The grouping also expressed concern over growing nuclear risks and conflict and reiterated the need to strengthen the system of disarmament, arms control and non-proliferation to promote global stability and international peace and security.Earlier, addressing the 18th BRICS Summit session on Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening in New Delhi, PM Modi proposed 10 measures for global governance reform, which BRICS members could develop into a BRICS Reform Roadmap by the next Summit.He also called for transforming the Global South from a ârule-taker into a rule-shaperâ, saying the Global South remains at the forefront of global crises but continues to remain on the sidelines when it comes to decision-making.

headline: Prime Minister Narendra Modi delivers closing remarks during the BRICS Session on 'Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism', at the 18th BRICS Summit at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi
full_text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi delivers closing remarks during the BRICS Session on 'Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism', at the 18th BRICS Summit at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi
NEW DELHI: The Brics countries have strongly condemned the Pahalgam terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir that killed 26 people, reaffirming their commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and calling for âzero toleranceâ towards the menace.The condemnation was included in the New Delhi Declaration 2026, adopted at the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi on Saturday.The declaration also opposed double standards in countering terrorism and called for concerted action against all UN-designated terrorists and terrorist entities.âWe express strong condemnation of any acts of terrorism as criminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation, whenever, wherever and by whomsoever committed,â the declaration said.It specifically condemned âin the strongest termsâ the terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir on April 22, 2025, during which 26 people were killed and several others injured.
Brics reaffirms stand against cross-border terror
The Brics declaration reaffirmed the groupingâs commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens.The grouping said terrorism should not be associated with any religion, nationality, civilisation or ethnic group.
It also stressed that those involved in terrorist activities and their support must be held accountable and brought to justice in accordance with relevant national and international law.The declaration called for âzero tolerance for terrorismâ and rejected double standards in countering terrorism.It also emphasised the primary responsibility of states in combating terrorism, while stressing that global efforts to prevent and counter terrorist threats must comply with international law, including the UN Charter and relevant international conventions and protocols.Brics welcomed the activities of its Counter-Terrorism Working Group and its five subgroups, which operate on the basis of the Brics Counter-Terrorism Strategy, Counter-Terrorism Action Plan and the Counter-Terrorism Working Group Position Paper.The grouping also called for the expeditious finalisation and adoption of the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism under the UN framework.The declaration further stressed the importance of countering extremism and radicalisation, particularly among younger generations, and called for greater cooperation among Brics countries and their competent authorities, including through the sharing of best practices.
Pahalgam attack and Indiaâs response
On April 22, last year, 26 civilians were killed in a terrorist attack in the Baisaran meadow area near Pahalgam in South Kashmir, a major tourist destination.The victims were segregated by the attackers based on religion before being shot in front of their families, triggering widespread outrage.Security forces launched search operations in the surrounding areas following the attack, while investigations were expanded to trace the terrorist network and its logistical support.India responded with âOperation Sindoorâ on May 7, 2025, carrying out precision strikes on terror infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.The operation marked a major escalation with Pakistan, followed by a four-day conflict that ended with a ceasefire on May 10, after Islamabadâs request.In the aftermath, Indian armed forces launched âOperation Mahadevâ and tracked down and eliminated the three attackers involved in the Pahalgam killings.
Declaration backs India, Brazil for greater UN role
Beyond terrorism, the New Delhi Declaration reaffirmed Brics' support for comprehensive reform of the United Nations, including the UN Security Council, with greater representation for developing countries.China and Russia, as permanent members of the UN Security Council, reiterated their support for the aspirations of India and Brazil to play a greater role in the UN, including its Security Council.The declaration called for greater and more meaningful participation and representation of emerging market and developing countries, as well as Least Developed Countries, in global decision-making processes.On Security Council reform, Brics said the process should make the body more democratic, representative, effective and efficient while increasing the representation of developing countries.âWe stress that the UN Security Council reform is to lead to the amplified voice of the Global South,â the declaration said.The grouping also called for equitable geographical representation in the UN Secretariat and other international organisations, particularly at senior and decision-making levels.
Brics raises concerns over trade measures
The declaration also expressed serious concern over unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures, saying they distort trade, threaten global supply chains and create uncertainty for international economic activity.Brics reaffirmed its support for reform of the World Trade Organization and called for an open, equitable, transparent, fair, inclusive, predictable and rules-based multilateral trading system, with the WTO at its core.The grouping also advocated the immediate restoration of an accessible, effective and fully functioning two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism and called for the appointment of new Appellate Body members without further delay.
On unilateral coercive measures, Brics condemned sanctions that it said were contrary to international law and reiterated its opposition to unilateral coercive measures, including those not authorised by the UN Security Council.The New Delhi Declaration was adopted during the 18th Brics Summit, being hosted by India on September 12-13 under its 2026 chairship. Indiaâs Brics chairship is guided by the theme âBuilding for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.â

headline: India is hosting the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, bringing together leaders from 11 member nations amidst global challenges, including West Asia conflicts and the unresolved India-China border dispute. Prime Minister Narendra Modi is scheduled to ...

India is hosting the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, bringing together leaders from 11 member nations amidst global challenges, including West Asia conflicts and the unresolved India-China border dispute. Prime Minister Narendra Modi is scheduled to hold key bilateral meetings, including talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping, following discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, and UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. As chair, India is prioritising the BRICS Economic Partnership 2030, expanding trade in services, building resilient supply chains following disruptions at critical transit routes like the Strait of Hormuz, and boosting financing for MSMEs. Additionally, on the sidelines of the summit, Prime Minister Modi presented a Russian translation of the ancient Tamil classic Tirukkural by philosopher Thiruvalluvar to President Putin, highlighting cultural diplomacy and historical literary connections between India and Russia.
India is hosting the eighteenth BRICS Summit, marking its chairship with over four hundred preparatory meetings centered on humanity first. The summit's core theme highlights four pillars: resilience, innovation, connectivity, and sustainability, alongside focused outreach to women and farmers. The eleven-member economic bloc represents forty percent of global GDP based on purchasing power parity and nearly fifty percent of the world's population. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's itinerary includes bilateral meetings with leaders from Ethiopia, Malaysia, Abu Dhabi, Vietnam, and China. In addition to diplomatic dialogues, leaders will participate in a sapling planting initiative at Bharat Mandapam, attend a cultural presentation featuring one hundred and sixty artists from member nations, and join a gala dinner. India has also proposed funding one hundred startups and prepared fifty outcome documents to deliver tangible solutions for international challenges.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to visit India for the BRICS Summit, marking his first visit to the country in seven years. The visit follows brief greetings at the Bishkek SCO Summit and a bilateral meeting in Tianjin in August 2025. Bilateral discussions are expected to focus on the border, trade, investment, and the broader relationship following the 2020 Galwan clash. Past diplomatic engagements between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping include the 2014 Ahmedabad visit, the 2015 Xi'an meeting, the 2018 Wuhan informal summit, and the 2019 Mamallapuram summit. The upcoming talks assess whether diplomatic relations can move towards stabilization.
India is hosting the 18th BRICS summit in New Delhi, bringing focus to key bilateral and multilateral dynamics. Ahead of the summit meetings, discussions highlight the significance of the engagement between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping following their border tensions. Key topics include managing border disputes, addressing the widening trade deficit where China remains India's largest trading partner, and securing greater market access for strategic sectors like batteries and clean energy infrastructure. The analysis covers the geopolitical role of the Russia-China-India triad, India's strategic multi-alignment, and the broader push for a multipolar global order. Representing nearly 2.8 billion people and 40 per cent of the global population, India and China continue to play a central role in shaping the Global South through platforms like BRICS, the G20, and the SCO, supported by long-standing civilisational ties.
Political discussions surrounding the BRICS summit focus on the upcoming bilateral engagement between India and China alongside broader geopolitical considerations. Discussions highlight that member nations seek economic resilience against external trade and military pressures without creating direct confrontation with the United States. Trade dynamics between the two countries involve industrial competitiveness, including supply chains where raw chemicals for generic pharmaceuticals are sourced from international suppliers. The dialogue addresses market access, historical trade impediments, and the spillover of border issues into economic relations. The multilateral platform brings together nations with divergent viewpoints to build consensus on shared economic interests and global leadership opportunities, reinforcing mutual diplomatic cooperation across upcoming summits.

headline: The adoption comes after reports of late-night negotiations that continued until 4 am, as India led efforts to bridge differences between the UAE and Iran.
full_text:
The adoption comes after reports of late-night negotiations that continued until 4 am, as India led efforts to bridge differences between the UAE and Iran.
NEW DELHI: The Brics countries on Saturday unanimously adopted the New Delhi Declaration 2026 at the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi. The 45-page declaration, comprising 140 points, was discussed under the theme âStrengthening Cooperation to Promote Fair Competition, including in Renewable Energy Marketsâ, with the aim of supporting sustainable energy transitions.âNo member has raised any objection. The New Delhi Declaration 2026 is adopted unanimously,â PM Modi said at the summit.The declaration focused on condemning terrorism, conflict prevention and peaceful resolution of disputes, stronger multilateralism and concerns over unilateral trade measures.
PM Modi, in his separate opening remarks, called for reforms in global governance and proposed 10 measures to be developed into a Brics reform roadmap. He also called for greater representation of the Global South in international decision-making, describing the existing system as a âpyramid of privilegeâ that should become a âplatform of partnershipâ.The declaration was adopted on the first day of the two-day Summit being hosted by India in New Delhi. The joint declaration came after intensive negotiations that continued until 4 am on Saturday, with India leading efforts to bridge differences between the UAE and Iran over the Middle East conflict.
The talks followed an earlier Brics foreign ministersâ meeting under Indiaâs presidency that ended without a consensus, prompting prolonged negotiations to ensure the summit resulted in a joint statement.India is chairing Brics in 2026 under the theme âBuilding for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainabilityâ.
Key points of the declaration
The Declaration addressed various key issues and concerns affecting the global order, such as:TerrorismBrics strongly condemned terrorism in all forms, including cross-border terrorism, terrorism financing and safe havens, condemned the April 22, 2025, terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir, and called for zero tolerance, accountability and early adoption of the UN Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism. "We reaffirm our commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens," it said."We reiterate that terrorism should not be associated with any religion, nationality, civilization or ethnic group and that all those involved in terrorist activities and their support must be held accountable and brought to justice in accordance with relevant national and international law," it continued, adding, ""We urge to ensure zero tolerance for terrorism and reject double standards in countering terrorism."Brics cooperationThe bloc reaffirmed its commitment to mutual respect, sovereign equality, solidarity, inclusiveness and consensus, and pledged to strengthen cooperation across its three pillars: political and security, economic and financial, and cultural and people-to-people cooperation. "We commend India for hosting the Outreach/BRICS Plus Dialogue segment of the 18thBRICS Summit, which injects new impetus to strengthen international cooperation andsolidarity," it further statedConflict preventionBrics countries stressed the importance of efforts to prevent conflicts, including by addressing their root causes. The declaration reaffirmed a commitment to resolving disputes through dialogue, consultation and diplomacy. Brics further urged all parties to uphold the Gaza ceasefire and ensure unhindered humanitarian aid, opposed the forced displacement of Palestinians, and reaffirmed support for a two-state solution with an independent Palestinian state based on the internationally recognised 1967 borders."We express deep concern over the âcontinued escalation of tensions in Middle East...call for exercising maximum restraint...avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation."Drugs and arms traffickingBrics expressed concern over illicit financial flows linked to drug-related crimes, firearms trafficking, terrorism financing and organised crime, and called for stronger cross-border cooperation to trace and disrupt criminal proceeds. âWe express our concerns about illicit financial flows including, financing of terrorism, trafficking of firearms, trafficking in persons, the laundering of drug related crimes proceeds,â the declaration said.Tariff concernsBrics voiced concern over unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures, warning they could hurt global trade and disrupt supply chains. âWe voice serious concerns about the rise of unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures which distort trade and are inconsistent with WTO rules,â the declaration said.It reaffirmed support for a WTO-centred multilateral trading system and called for the immediate restoration of a âfully functioning, two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanismâ, along with the appointment of new Appellate Body members. The bloc also condemned unilateral economic and secondary sanctions. âWe condemn the imposition of unilateral coercive measures that are contrary to international law,â the declaration said, calling for their elimination as they âundermine international law and the principles and purposes of the UN Charter.âIt also backed Ethiopia and Iranâs WTO membership bids and noted Chinaâs move to extend zero-tariff treatment to 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic ties.Energy security and transitionThe declaration called for stronger energy security through diversified energy sources, resilient infrastructure and stable markets, while recognising that fossil fuels will continue to play an important role, particularly for emerging and developing economies. âWe acknowledge fossil fuels will still play an important role in the world's energy mix, particularly for emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs),â it said. It also backed âjust, orderly, equitable and inclusive energy transitionsâ and a technology-neutral approach covering renewables, nuclear energy, hydropower, hydrogen, fossil fuels and low-carbon technologies.Womenâs empowermentBrics recognised women as leaders, decision-makers and drivers of economic growth and social transformation, stressing their participation in governance, economic life, peacebuilding and climate action."We affirm that women's participation in governance; their financial and digital inclusion; their capacity building, access to skill development and entrepreneurship opportunities, support to entrepreneurship, access to productive and social services and their crucial role in climate action, food security and nutrition, which are interconnected is key for sustainable development," the declaration said."We also recognise the importance of policies that support women's full participation in economic life, including through appropriate care policies, in accordance with national circumstances," the leaders further said.Local currencies' pushBrics backed efforts to promote cross-border payments and trade settlements using member countriesâ local currencies, while respecting national priorities. âWe acknowledge the work done to study the cross-border interoperability of payment and messaging channels, and the discussions on promoting trade settlements and investments using BRICS local currencies,â the declaration stated.Supporting India's role in UNSCBrics reaffirmed support for reform of the UN, including the Security Council, to make it more democratic and representative and give developing countries a greater role. China and Russia, as permanent members of the Security Council, reiterated their support for Brazil and India to play a greater role in the UN, including its Security Council. âChina and Russia, as permanent members of the UN Security Council, reiterate their support to the aspirations of Brazil and India to play a greater role in the UN, including its Security Council,â the declaration said.
Sports technologyBrics recognised the growing role of technology in improving sports performance, athlete welfare, governance and inclusion, and encouraged greater cooperation among member countries through exchanges of good practices, technical information and research. âWe welcome the proposal for the BRICS Sports Goods Manufacturing Conclave to promote cooperation in sports goods manufacturing, research and innovation,â the declaration stated. It also encouraged discussions on forming a dedicated Working Group on Sports Technology.
